extracted.intended_audience: humanities PhDs, junior faculty, and academic job applicants seeking grant strategy and CV/grant pitching advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, career-oriented guidance on how to present and pursue grants in the humanities — how to list grants on a CV, shape the research statement as a grant pitch, target funders by career year, and avoid common proposal mistakes. Emphasis is on early-career/junior faculty preparing for tenure and grant competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants on the CV (external vs internal)
rubrics_metrics.description: External grants matter more than internal grants; federal/foundation grants matter more than university seed grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List grants by total dollar amount and include PI/Co-PI status. Prioritize and emphasize external (federal, foundation) awards over internal university seed grants when presenting grant record on an academic CV.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to list pending or unsuccessful submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Submitted but not funded" should generally be listed only if competitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include unfunded submissions when they were competitive (e.g., advanced to external review or a small/major national competition). Avoid cluttering the CV with numerous 'submitted but not funded' entries that signal low success rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer/service roles as evidence of seniority
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer service for funders signals seniority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List reviewer or panel service for grant organizations as part of evidence of professional reputation and standing; it helps demonstrate that you are trusted by funders and contributes to perceived seniority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research statement should open with the big question
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with the big question, not the methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the research statement with a compelling, conceptual question or problem rather than a methods-heavy lead. This frames the significance and intellectual stakes before describing methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research statement should show scholarly progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Show progression from dissertation to current to future work; the 'future work' section IS your future grant pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrate how past work (dissertation), current projects, and future plans form a coherent trajectory. Use the future-work portion to signal fundable projects and align with prospective funders' priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name potential funders in research/plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Include at least 2-3 named potential funders; demonstrate awareness of funding landscape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly name appropriate agencies, foundations, or programs you would target for the project; this shows strategic planning and realism about where support might come from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Junior faculty staged grant strategy (year-by-year)
rubrics_metrics.description: First year: write 2-3 small grants ($5-50K); Second year: target a major external grant (NSF, NEH, foundation); Third year: have at least one funded major grant. Tenure clock: 5-6 years means grants must be in pipeline immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat grant-seeking as a staged pipeline aligned with the tenure clock. Early, small awards build credibility leading to larger external awards; begin applying immediately upon starting a tenure-track job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mellon funder priorities (humanities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mellon: long-term, transformative, often institutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mellon awards favor projects with institutional reach, long-term engagement, and transformative potential rather than short-term smaller-scope projects. Frame proposals around systemic impact and institutional partnerships where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEH funder priorities (humanities)
rubrics_metrics.description: NEH: clear public humanities angle helps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals to NEH should highlight public-facing significance, broader public impact, and how humanities scholarship connects to public audiences or civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACLS funder priorities (humanities)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACLS: strong scholarly contribution within established field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACLS favors projects that make a rigorous, demonstrable scholarly contribution within disciplinary norms; emphasize originality and deep engagement with the scholarly literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSRC funder priorities (humanities/social science)
rubrics_metrics.description: SSRC: comparative, international, social-science methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSRC prizes comparative and international perspectives and projects employing social-science methods; position work to speak across regions and to social-scientific debates where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common application mistakes to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Junior faculty applying for senior fellowships; senior faculty applying for junior fellowships; grant proposals that read like dissertation chapters; no engagement with current scholarship; vague timeline / no clear deliverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match fellowship/program level to career stage. Avoid submitting projects that are simply reworked dissertation chapters; clearly engage contemporary scholarship; provide a detailed timeline with concrete deliverables (avoid vague or overly ambitious schedules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Clear, novel argument or contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, novel argument or contribution to field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders look for projects that articulate a specific, novel intellectual contribution — not a vague claim of importance. Explicitly state what is new and why it matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Demonstrated mastery of relevant scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrated mastery of relevant scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show deep knowledge of the literature and situate your project within existing debates; reviewers expect familiarity with key works and current conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Realistic, appropriate methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Realistic methodology (archives, fieldwork, interviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe methods that are suitable and feasible for the research questions (e.g., archival research, fieldwork, interviews). Avoid proposing methods that are mismatched to the goals or overly speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Clear timeline with checkpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear timeline with checkpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a detailed timeline delineating phases, milestones, and deliverables (e.g., archival visits, chapter drafts, outreach activities) to convince reviewers the project will be completed as proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Evidence project will produce a substantial output
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence the project will produce a book or comparable output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate concrete scholarly outputs (book, article series, digital resource) and how project activities map onto those outputs to make the case for fundability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Strong letters of support from senior scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong letters of support from senior scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure recommenders who are senior and credible in the field and who can speak specifically to the project's feasibility and the applicant's capacity to execute it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Career-stage fit with funder
rubrics_metrics.description: Career stage match for the funder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the project aligns with the targeted funder's intended career stage (e.g., early-career fellowships vs senior awards); mismatch undermines competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty: Vague claims of importance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Important new work on X" without specifying the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic claims of importance; specify the precise contribution, novelty, and measurable outcomes of the proposed research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty: Methodology disguised as question
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology that's actually a research question disguised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't present research questions as if they were methods. Clearly define methods and show how they will answer the research questions; reviewers expect methodological clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty: Unrealistic timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Unrealistic timeline (a book in one year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about how long research activities and writing will take. Overly compressed schedules are a common red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty: No engagement with logistics (e.g., archives)
rubrics_metrics.description: No engagement with archival access logistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address practical access issues (archives, permissions, fieldwork approvals) and contingency plans so reviewers believe the work is feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty: Letters from too-junior referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters from too-junior referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain recommenders of appropriate seniority who can credibly attest to your qualifications and the project's significance; junior letter-writers can weaken an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty: Mismatch with funder's stated priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mismatch with funder's stated priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor proposals to the specific priorities and missions of targeted funders; failure to align is a frequent reason for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants as part of an ecosystem
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants are part of an ecosystem; one grant signals capacity for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that small awards build the track record that helps secure larger grants later. Frame funding history as evidence of trajectory and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply early and often
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply early and often; rejection is the norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a high-volume, consistent submission rhythm to increase chances of success. Expect rejections and treat them as part of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use program officers strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Use program officers strategically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact program officers to discuss fit and receive informal feedback before applying; they can advise on whether a proposal aligns with program priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network via grant-writing workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Network through grant-writing workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend workshops to improve proposals and build relationships with peers and mentors who can provide feedback and collaboration opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a grant-writing habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a 'grant-writing habit' of one application per quarter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish regular, scheduled effort on grant-writing (e.g., aiming for one application per quarter) to generate a steady pipeline of submissions and improve craft through practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter / project summary best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Hook with the question, not your methods; position yourself as the right person; be specific about contribution; don't oversell; match length to instructions exactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a concise project summary that opens with the intellectual question or hook, clearly states the contribution, explains why you are the appropriate investigator, avoids hyperbole, and adheres strictly to length/format requirements in the funder's instructions.
